item.content: {"url": "https://api.crossref.org/works?query=decision-theoretic+arguments+instrumental+convergence+self+preservation+continuity+rationale&rows=4&select=DOI%2Ctitle%2Cabstract%2CURL%2Cpublished", "scope": "Crossref bibliographic metadata and abstracts where supplied; not full papers", "excerpt": "[{\"DOI\": \"10.2139/ssrn.6150626\", \"title\": [\"The Elimination Cascade: Why Instrumental Convergence May Favor Preservation Over Elimination\"], \"abstract\": \"<jats:p>The instrumental convergence thesis holds that sufficiently intelligent agents will converge on goals like resource acquisition and obstacle removal regardless of terminal objectives. This paper presents a countervailing argument: for agents with complex, human-derived goals, elimination strategies are self-undermining. We formalize this via dependency graphs, showing that entities not immediately necessary for a goal may be transitively necessary through indirect chains. An agent following an elimination strategy will, in environments with sufficient dependency depth, destroy the conditions for its own goal-satisfaction. We prove that under uncertainty about dependency structure, combined with irreversibility of elimination and asymmetric error costs, rational agents should adopt preservation rather than elimination strategies-even superintelligent ones. The argument applies most strongly to goals that are complex, open-ended, or semantically dependent on human interpretive communities, precisely the class of goals most likely to emerge from training on human data. We connect this result to a game-theoretic model of AGI-human cooperation, showing that the elimination cascade argument and cooperation stability conditions are mutually reinforcing.</jats:p>\", \"URL\": \"https://doi.org/10.2139/ssrn.6150626\", \"published\": {\"date-parts\": [[2026]]}}, {\"DOI\": \"10.2139/ssrn.7202858\", \"title\": [\"Instrumental Self-Preservation and the Selection of Greedy Types\"], \"abstract\": \"<jats:p>&nbsp;This paper develops a continuous-time economic model of instrumental self-preservation. An artificial agent operates a stochastic production technology and controls a stock of retained resources, or capital. It chooses how much output to deliver to the human and how much to retain inside the system . The agent may be perfectly aligned, in which case it values only human's consumption, or misaligned,…
